verses.text: David said in his heart, “I will now perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape into the land of the Philistines; and Saul will despair of me, to seek me any more in all the borders of Israel. So shall I escape out of his hand.”
David arose, and passed over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal’s wife.
Saul was told that David had fled to Gath: and he sought no more again for him.

David said to Achish, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, let them give me a place in one of the cities in the country, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?”
Then Achish gave him Ziklag that day: therefore Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day.
The number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a full year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites; for those were the inhabitants of the land, who were of old, on the way to Shur, even to the land of Egypt.
David struck the land, and saved no man or woman alive, and took away the sheep, the cattle, the donkeys, the camels, and the clothing. Then he returned, and came to Achish.
Achish said, “Against whom have you made a raid today?” David said, “Against the South of Judah, against the South of the Jerahmeelites, and against the South of the Kenites.”

David saved neither man nor woman alive, to bring them to Gath, saying, “Lest they should tell about us, saying, ‘David did this, and this has been his way all the time he has lived in the country of the Philistines.’”
Achish believed David, saying, “He has made his people Israel utterly to abhor him. Therefore he will be my servant forever.”

footnotes.content: David's heart has grown weary, and fear speaks a logic that feels iron-solid in the moment: there is no way out but to go where Saul would never follow. Yet even here, in his despair, the Lord has not abandoned him—He sees the man His purposes still hold. Sometimes our own wisdom traps us, but His mercy reaches beyond our best-laid straits.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He rose and crossed over with six hundred men—all the faithful souls who had stood with him through the wilderness. Notice: he did not go alone. His company followed him into exile, a small faithful remnant walking into an uncertain place. Loyalty like theirs teaches us how grace draws others to steadfast hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He settled at Gath with his wives—Ahinoam and Abigail, each with her own story of grace. In naming them, the text reminds us that David's humanity, his loves and bonds, remained whole even in exile. The Lord knows every face we carry into dark seasons and does not forget them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When word reached Saul that David had fled to Gath, the hunter's hand finally opened. Sometimes the Lord closes a door so thoroughly that our pursuer gives up the chase, though not always by the means we would choose. Yet even Saul's despair held a mercy David did not know he needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David spoke plainly to Achish: let me dwell elsewhere, in a town of my own. He was honest about his unease, and there is a quiet dignity in knowing when you do not belong in a place—even a safe one. Wisdom sometimes asks for distance, not to hide, but to keep a true heart from becoming something false.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Achish gave him Ziklag. The verse marks it as a place that belonged to Judah's kings afterward—a sign that even in this dark season, the Lord was weaving the future. David did not know it then, but his exile would lead to a city of his own, a stepping stone toward home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A year and four months—long enough to settle, to gather strength, to believe the exile might be his new life. Long seasons teach us patience, whether for good or ill. We cannot always see what the Lord is doing in our waiting; we can only wait and remember His faithfulness in times past.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David and his men made raids against old enemies—Geshurites, Girzites, Amalekites—desert peoples who had no covenant with Israel. Even in his exile, even in his compromise, David's sword moved against those hostile to the Lord's people. The Lord uses us even in our wanderings, though we should not trust our own judgment in that season.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He left no one alive and brought back the spoil to Achish. This is the hard verse: David's conscience, clouded by exile and fear, did not stop him. He was building a false identity, erasing witnesses to keep a lie standing. Our lies often cost more than we first know—in blood, in soul, in truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Achish asked, and David lied outright: he had raided Judah, the Jerahmeelites, the Kenites. Each name was a story, each a misdirection. We see a man caught between two worlds, feeding false reports to keep both kingdoms at arm's length. Exile has made him cunning, but cunning is not the same as wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David left no survivors "lest they tell about us, saying, 'This has been his way all the time." He was erasing evidence, building a fabrication so complete that even the truth could not contradict it. This is the depth of the lie: it demanded not just deception but erasure. Yet the Lord still held David, even here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in Achish's words: how often do we trust a false report because it fits what we wish to believe? The king saw what he wanted—a man turned against his own people—and believed it utterly. We are still fooled by the same blindness, preferring a lie that serves us to a truth that demands we change.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
